newsitem.title: THAILAND: Finance crisis, Moody's keep Thai economy on edge.
newsitem.headline: Finance crisis, Moody's keep Thai economy on edge.

text.p: A crisis in the finance sector and worries about a looming credit rating downgrade by Moody's Investors Service will keep Thailand's economy edgy for the near term, analysts said on Tuesday.

Although some analysts see cyclical recovery on the way, most said the next three months would be crucial for Thai authorities grappling with a crisis of confidence crisis among investors, a liquidity crunch squeezing financial institutions and high interest rates.
Unless liquidity problems were eased, the baht and high rates were stabilised and sluggish exports showed improvement in that time, the economy faced a rough road ahead, they said.
"These are three key issues that I think the government will have to watch closely," said Arporn Chewakrengkai, chief economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Thailand.
"If we bode well during this tough time, things should be alright as the fundamentals remain good. But if not, Thailand could be at risk of becoming the sick man of Asia," she said.

On Monday, the authorities disclosed that 10 finance firms were in urgent need of capital increases due to liquidity problems and told banks and finance firms to raise provisions to make up for bad loans, mainly to the troubled property sector.
Analysts said the admission by the authorities of problems in the finance sector, after earlier rumours and denials, had shaken investor confidence in Thai regulators.
On Tuesday, banks and finance stocks were sold heavily on the bourse forcing the stock index down by over three percent.

Economists from U.S. rationgs firm Moody's Investors Service Inc are due in Bangkok this week to study economic data before the agency makes a decision on whether or not to downgrade Thailand's long term sovereign debt ratings.

A mid-February Moody's statement that it had put Thai ratings on watch for a possible downgrade was already a negative for the Thai economy as Thai firms would have to pay a higher premium to raise money abroad if the rating was cut.

Analysts see Thailand's economy, which enjoyed a decade of nearly nine percent growth annually until 1995, slowing sharply this year to below six percent amid a major slowdown in exports due to structural and cyclical factors.
This compares with central bank projections of 6.7 percent growth for this year and 6.8 percent in 1997.
Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan ordered nearly 100 billion baht ($3.8 billion) in spending cuts in early-February to try to narrow a wide current account deficit.

The wide current account deficit, which stood at 8.0 percent of gross domestic product in 1996, compounded by jitters about the health of finance firms, pressure from a strong dollar and devaluation talk sparked speculator attacks on the baht.
The baht has steadied after Thailand ruled out devaluation and dollar pressure on the currency eased, dealers said.

But the stock market remains spooked by worries that earnings of financial institutions would be squeezed hard this year by the higher provisioning against bad loans and by a depression in the property sector.
However, analysts sees some rays of hope in measures taken by the authorities to cut spending, restructure taxes to boost exports and assure the property sector of help when in need.
"Compared to what the Japanese are experiencing, this wake-up call (for Thailand) has come about at very low cost," said Wong Yit Fan, chief regional economist at Standard Chartered.
Exports would be the most important factor to propel growth this year as consumption and investment has slowed.
"We forecast exports this year will improve with a regional cyclical upturn around the corner, Thailand should follow the trend," said Supavud Saicheua, Phatra Research chief economist.
US$1 = 25.8 baht
